title: The last arrow
hook: Agastya's mantra; the sun; Ravana falls

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ravana rides out, and the heads that kept growing back. Your line was name a head. Which one did you name? Day sixty-six.

The last week of a hard job. The last night in the hospital. The last exam. Near the end of something long, it gets hard to tell whether you're winning at all. The fight between Rama and Ravana has gone on and on. The gods have sent Rama a chariot, Indra's own, driven by Indra's charioteer, Matali. Ravana's heads keep growing back. And Rama, in Valmiki's telling, is worn out, and worried. Then an old sage walks onto the battlefield. Agastya. And instead of a weapon, he gives Rama words.
screen: `THE END OF SOMETHING LONG.` → `HEADS THAT KEEP GROWING BACK.` → `A SAGE WALKS ONTO THE FIELD.`

segments.voice: Agastya teaches Rama a hymn to the sun. It's called the Aditya Hridayam, the heart of the sun. Praise the sun, the sage tells him, the one who lights every world and wakes every living thing. Recite this, and fear and grief will leave you. So, in the middle of a war, Rama stops. He looks at the sun. He recites the hymn, and in the story, strength comes back into him. Devotees still chant this hymn, some at sunrise, some before a hard day: the words a tired prince heard on a battlefield. Then Matali, the charioteer, speaks up. Remember the weapon made by Brahma, he says. The time has come. And Rama takes out an arrow given to him long before: the brahmastra, the weapon of the creator himself. He sets it to the bow and releases it. It strikes Ravana in the chest, in the heart, and the king of Lanka falls from his chariot. The gods rain flowers. The war is over. Later tellings, Tulsidas's among them, add a detail: that Ravana kept a store of nectar in his navel, and Vibhishana told Rama where to aim. Valmiki's version doesn't have it; there the weapon itself does the work. Both agree on what matters. The last arrow didn't come from trying harder. It came after Rama stopped, turned toward the light, and steadied himself. And then something just as important: it ends. Wars in stories can feel endless. This one had a last day.
screen: `THE HEART OF THE SUN.` · `RAMA STOPS AND TURNS TO THE LIGHT.` · `THE BRAHMASTRA: THE LAST ARROW.` · `RAVANA FALLS. IT ENDS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and if you can see daylight, turn toward it, or picture the sun on your face. Think of a long fight that finally ended for you. An illness, a hard season, a conflict with someone, a year you thought would never finish. It did. Let yourself feel that it's over, if you never stopped long enough to feel it. And if you're in the middle of one now, just take this one thing from Rama: stop for a moment, turn toward the light, and breathe. It will end. The bell holds the time.
Aditya Hridayam, the heart of the sun, the hymn Agastya gives Rama before the last arrow, the weapon made by Brahma, ends the war in Lanka.
Your line: it ends. Today, if you're in something long, look up at the sky once, and remind yourself: it ends. Day sixty-six.

howItsDone: Devotees chant the Aditya Hridayam, the hymn Agastya teaches Rama, at sunrise or before difficult undertakings; Ravana's defeat is celebrated at Dussehra (Vijayadashami), when effigies of Ravana are burned in many towns.

fork.setup: you're Rama. you're exhausted, the heads keep growing back, and an old sage offers you a hymn to the sun. what do you do?
options: stop, face the sun, and recite it.
fork.reveal: he stops in the middle of the war and recites it. strength returns, and then the last arrow ends the fight.

original.note: Sanskrit: aditya (the sun) + hridayam (heart). 'The heart of the sun', Agastya's hymn.

trapdoor: what you thought: the hero fires the killing shot.
what it means: before the last arrow, the hero stops in the middle of a war and turns toward the light.
what a scholar hears: the Aditya Hridayam sits in the Yuddha Kanda; some scholars think it was added later, and it is widely chanted on its own.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (Agastya's Aditya Hridayam; Matali's counsel; the brahmastra; Ravana's death, roughly sargas 105–108)
Tulsidas, Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand (the nectar in Ravana's navel)

notes: The Aditya Hridayam is paraphrased, not quoted; confirm the paraphrase ('fear and grief will leave you') fairly reflects it.
Some critical editions treat the Aditya Hridayam as a later addition; the trapdoor says 'some scholars think it was added later'. Confirm.
The nectar-in-the-navel detail is attributed to later tellings (Tulsidas, and others); confirm.
Matali reminding Rama of the brahmastra given by Agastya follows Valmiki as remembered; confirm.
